result.summary: The Argive host marches out amid tearful farewells, and the poet catalogues its contingents and leaders. Thebes prepares fearfully, and Tiresias raises the ghosts of the dead, among them Laius, who prophesies victory for Thebes. Bacchus then dries up the rivers to delay the Argives, who find water only through Hypsipyle, who leads them to the stream of Langia.

scenes.title: War begins; farewells at Argos
scenes.summary: Bellona hurls her spear and arms the camp. Families weep and cling to the departing soldiers.
scenes.stakes: Warriors and families face parting and death in war.

scenes.title: Catalogue of the Argive host
scenes.summary: The poet invokes Calliope and lists the contingents of Adrastus, Polynices, Tydeus, Hippomedon and Capaneus.
scenes.stakes: The army marches toward a war many are fated to lose.

scenes.title: Eriphyle's gold; Amphiaraus and Arcadians
scenes.summary: Eriphyle takes Harmonia's necklace from Argia, Amphiaraus joins the march, and Laconian, Elean and Arcadian contingents follow, led by Parthenopaeus.
scenes.stakes: Amphiaraus is doomed by his wife's greed.

scenes.title: Atalanta pleads with her son
scenes.summary: Atalanta runs from the woods and begs Parthenopaeus to stay home. She cannot restrain him and commends him to Adrastus.
scenes.stakes: She fears losing her young son in war.

scenes.title: Fearful Thebes
scenes.summary: Thebes arms reluctantly amid rumours, and a frenzied Bacchante prophesies. The king consults Tiresias.

scenes.title: Tiresias raises the dead
scenes.summary: Tiresias and Manto perform necromancy. Manto describes the Theban ghosts, and Laius prophesies Theban victory but a curse on Oedipus' sons.
scenes.stakes: Thebes' fate and the sons of Oedipus hang on the ghosts' prophecy.

scenes.title: Bacchus dries the rivers
scenes.summary: Bacchus, seeing the Argives near, orders the nymphs to hide the waters. Drought afflicts the army, and Adrastus meets Hypsipyle with the infant Opheltes.
scenes.stakes: The Argive army faces death from thirst.

scenes.title: The army finds water
scenes.summary: Hypsipyle guides the host to Langia's stream, where the soldiers drink wildly and praise the river.

alias_notes.explanation: Latin cult name of the wine god.
Name meaning 'beginning of doom' given after his death.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of families' tearful farewells to departing warriors.
Eriphyle's betrayal for gold seals her husband's fate.

analysis.text: Greed, fate and family guilt drive the war: Eriphyle's bribe, Laius' curse and Oedipus' sons' rivalry.
The catalogue of contingents imitates Homer's Catalogue of Ships and displays Roman-era learning in local geography.

legacy.text: Statius' necromancy scene and Hypsipyle episode influenced later epic and Dante's use of the Thebaid.

fun_facts.text: Statius wrote under the Roman emperor Domitian in the late first century AD.

language_notes.text: 'Thrice had Phoebus loosened stark winter' means three winters had passed since the quarrel at Thebes began; the sun god Phoebus brings the spring.
Bellona is the Roman goddess of war; Larissa is the citadel of Argos; 'Aonian Dirce' means Thebes, since Dirce is a Theban spring and Aonia a name for Boeotia.
Gradivus is an epithet of Mars, the war god; Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry.
Arion is the famous swift horse of Adrastus, said to be born of Neptune.
The Eumenides are the Furies; Phlegethon is a river of fire in the underworld. The list of crimes refers to Thracian, Mycenaean and Theban family horrors.
The 'Gorgon-quelling steed' is Pegasus, whose hoof struck out a spring; Ino was the Theban queen who became a sea goddess.
The Sphinx on Polynices' sword recalls the monster of Thebes, which Oedipus defeated; the lion skin recalls the lion he wore when he came to Argos.
Jove loved Io, daughter of the river god Inachus, so the river is called 'swollen with Jove, his daughter's lover'.
Thamyris, a Thracian singer, challenged the Muses and was struck dumb and robbed of his skill; the Satyr is Marsyas, who lost a contest to Apollo.
Atropos is the Fate who cuts the thread of life; here she overpowers Amphiaraus's prophetic foresight, so he goes to war knowing he will die.
The 'gift' is Harmonia's necklace, cursed since its making. Polynices gave it to Eriphyle, who sold her husband's life for it.
Cyllarus was Castor's famous horse; 'Taenarian' refers to Taenarum in Laconia. These horses are of his breed, sired on lesser mares.
Fillet: a band of cloth worn round the head, here a sacred mark of the priestly prophet.
The conquered Python on his shield recalls Apollo's slaying of the serpent at Delphi; Apollo is Amphiaraus's patron god.
The Arcadian god is Mars here, said to train the Spartan-style Laconian youth; 'naked valour' refers to lightly armed, bare-shouldered fighting.
A Ledaean crest: helmet crests of Leda's sons, Castor and Pollux, the Spartan heroes.
The Alpheus was said to run under the sea to Sicily (Sicanian lands) without mixing with salt water.
Oenomaus, king of Pisa, raced and killed suitors of his daughter in chariots until Pelops beat him; Elis kept its horse-breeding fame.
Parthenopaeus's warlike mother is Atalanta, huntress and devotee of Diana, who is away hunting while he leaves.
Arcadians were said to be older than the moon, and born from trees; the myth marks them as primeval, autochthonous people.
Mycenae stayed out because of the feud of Atreus and Thyestes, whose banquet of children made the sun turn back.
"Tidings" means news; "a captain" means he is going as a commander. "O'er" is poetic for "over."
She presses her breast against the reins, blocking his horse by standing in its path.
"Shafts" are arrows; "nought" means nothing. She says her hunting gear will be useless in real war.
Erymanthian Nymphs: nymphs of Mount Erymanthus in Arcadia. She means he is too young even for love affairs.
Omens: shaking temples and fallen votive offerings were read as signs of divine displeasure. Diana is the huntress goddess Atalanta serves.
"The shadow come upon thy rosy cheeks" means the first beard; she wants him to wait until he is grown.
"Born of rock and oak" alludes to the old belief that early peoples sprang from stones and trees, meaning hard-hearted.
"Martian folk of Cadmus" means the Thebans, Cadmus's people, called Martian because they sprang from the dragon's teeth sacred to Mars, god of war.
Amphion raised Thebes' walls by playing his lyre, so that the stones moved into place of their own accord. Hence "inspired harp".
Lerna is a marsh near Argos, used here for Argive forces. Asopus, Cithaeron, Teumesos and Plataeae are Boeotian rivers, mountains and towns.
The Sphinx was the riddling monster Oedipus defeated at Thebes. Her reappearance would be a terrible omen.
"Ogygian" means Theban, after Ogyges, a legendary early king of the region.
A thyrsus is Bacchus's staff, wreathed in ivy and tipped with a pine cone. Here it is imagined as iron-pointed, a weapon.
"Clear-sighted blindness" is a paradox: Tiresias was physically blind but saw the future.
Heaven's will is read through standard divination (sacrifice, bird flight, entrails, tripod oracles, astrology, altar smoke); the seer claims necromancy is clearer than all of these.
Latonia means Diana, daughter of Latona. Here she haunts the grove as a shadowy underworld goddess, not the huntress.
Her uncle's threshold is the house of Dis (Pluto), the underworld, where she serves as Hecate before returning as Diana.
The Martian plain is where Cadmus sowed the dragon's teeth, and armed men sprang up and killed one another.
Sons of earth are the Sparti, the armed men grown from the dragon's teeth; their ghostly fighting still haunts the field.
Attic rain probably means honey-water; Attic honey was famous. The note marks it as a libation offering.
The daughter of Perses is Hecate; the cloud-wrapt Arcadian is Mercury, guide of souls.
The Gortynian judge is Minos of Crete, who judges the dead in the underworld.
Sisyphus's rock, Tantalus's waters, Tityos and Ixion are the famous punishments of the damned.
The Colchian maiden is Medea, the sorceress from Colchis; Circe lived on the island of Aeaea. Both were famed enchantresses, though here Manto lacks their crimes.
Cadmus, founder of Thebes, and his wife Harmonia (daughter of Venus, called Cytherea) were later turned into serpents, hence the twin snakes.
The earth-born company are the Sparti, warriors who sprang from dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus; they fought each other and lived only a day.
Pentheus was torn apart by Bacchic women, including his mother Agave, in a frenzy sent by Bacchus; Echion was his father.
Aristaeus' son is Actaeon, turned into a stag for seeing Diana bathing and killed by his own hounds.
The Tantalid is Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, who boasted of her many children over Latona and lost them all.
Pelops was maimed (an ivory shoulder replaced the one eaten by Ceres); Oenomaus was killed in a chariot race with Pelops, dying in the dust.
The fifty are the Theban warriors who ambushed Tydeus and were all killed but one, Maeon.
Aonian means Boeotian, i.e. Theban; Tiresias is a Theban seer.
Oedipus killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta, returning to the place of his own begetting.
Gradivus is Mars; sons of Lerna are the Argives; unlawful withholding from the fire refers to the denial of burial to the dead.
Sons of Inachus: the Argives, named for Inachus, the first king and river-god of Argos. Sidonian here means Theban, from Cadmus's Phoenician origin.
Liber is a Latin name for Bacchus; Haemus, Othrys and Rhodope are Thracian and Thessalian mountains; Icarian shade means vine shade, from Icarius, who received the vine from Dionysus.
The stepmother is Juno, who persecuted Bacchus as the child of Jupiter and Semele, the Theban princess his mother.
Bacchus recalls Semele's death: she asked to see Jupiter in his glory and was consumed by his lightning, and Bacchus was born from the fire.
The heat-bringing hound is the Dog Star, tied to the Icarian myth of Erigone and her father's dog; its rising brought summer's fiercest heat.
Horn-footed ones are satyrs, and Fauns are lustful woodland spirits; Bacchus offers to restrain them as a reward to the nymphs.
Syene is a southern Egyptian city on the Nile, a byword for cloudless heat; Amymone is a spring at Lerna.
Adrastus guesses Hypsipyle is a goddess made fruitful by Jupiter, who often visited mortal women, citing his Argive loves such as Io and Danae.
The Crab is the zodiac sign Cancer, marking midsummer heat, and the Icarian star is the Dog Star, with its blazing coat.
The Berecyntian mother is Cybele; the Curetes drowned the cries of the infant Jupiter on Mount Ide with their clashing, to hide him from Saturn.
"Mien" means bearing or manner; here Hypsipyle walks with a proud, dignified air.
Ambracian sea is the Ambracian Gulf in western Greece; Leucas is an island nearby, marked by a temple of Apollo on its headland, which sailors greeted.
"Levelling thirst" means thirst that erases rank, treating chieftain and common soldier alike.
Hercules strangled the Nemean lion, whose haunt was this same Nemea; the speaker says the land is crueller to the army than the lion was to him.
"Corus" is the northwest wind, bringer of storms; "horned one" refers to the river god's traditional horned image.
Ladon, Xanthus, Spercheus and Lycormas are famous rivers of Arcadia, Troy, Thessaly and Aetolia; the speaker ranks this stream above them.

context_notes.text: Reading the entrails of sacrificed animals was how a priest judged whether the gods favoured an undertaking; here the omens are bad.
Polynices is Adrastus' son-in-law, an exile from Thebes who has come to Argos to win back his share of the kingship.
Tydeus, son of Oeneus, is the Aetolian hero who also married a daughter of Adrastus and joins the war on Polynices' behalf.
Hippomedon's shield shows the daughters of Danaus, who murdered their husbands on their wedding night; Danaus was an ancient king of Argos.
Capaneus is a giant warrior who despises the gods; his shield shows Hercules' victory over the Hydra of Lerna.
Tisiphone is one of the Furies, here driving the house of Oedipus's allies toward ruin and delighting in the coming war.
Parthenopaeus is a beautiful young Arcadian, son of Atalanta, who joins the Seven against Thebes against his mother's wishes.
Diana is goddess of the hunt and of chaste companions; her forgiving a love-struck companion shows his special favor.
Atalanta is the famed huntress of Arcadia, a devotee of Diana; her son Parthenopaeus joins the Argive army marching against Thebes.
Adrastus is king of Argos and leader of the expedition against Thebes, so she entrusts her son to him.
Nysa is the mountain of Bacchus's upbringing. Bacchus (Dionysus) was born of the Theban princess Semele, so Thebes is his ancestral land.
Bacchus is asked to carry the Bacchante to the far north, away from the horrors she foresees in the ruling house of Thebes.
The two bulls stand for the brothers Eteocles and Polynices, who are fighting over the throne of Thebes.
Tiresias is the blind Theban seer; the grove is a sacred wood beside the Ismenos river near Thebes.
The son of Oedipus is Eteocles's brother Polynices, or in this scene a fearful Theban leader attending the rite.
Tiresias was blinded in myth, and gained prophetic sight in compensation; here he says he once saw the underworld.
Manto is Tiresias' daughter and guide; they conduct a necromantic rite to summon the dead for prophecy before the Argive attack on Thebes.
Laius, Oedipus' father and former king of Thebes, was killed by his own son; his shade hates his grandsons, Eteocles and Polynices.
Lachesis is one of the Fates; Megaera is a Fury. Laius speaks only so far as they allow.
Epic poets invoke a Muse or god for inspiration. Statius addresses Phoebus (Apollo) and pleads that his own knowledge of the tale is thin.
Archemorus is the other name given to Opheltes after his death, when the Nemean Games were founded in his honour.
Hypsipyle, a former queen of Lemnos, is now a slave nursing Opheltes, the son of Lycurgus, priest of Nemea.
Hypsipyle was exiled from Lemnos after saving her father from the women's massacre of the men there; her own sons were left behind.
Argus is one of the Argive captains marching against Thebes; Hypsipyle is leading the thirsty army to water.
Nemea was sacred to Jove, and the army is stranded there by drought; Hercules's first labour was killing the Nemean lion.
Lycormas is called a river of Centaur's fame, linked to the Centaur Nessus, whom Hercules killed at a river crossing.

literary_notes.text: The long comparison of farewells to a ship departing helps the reader feel the lingering grief of the families, drawing out the moment.
Adrastus is compared to an old bull, still the leader though his strength has gone; his scars give him authority.
Tydeus is compared to a snake that has shed its skin in spring, showing his renewed vigour and the danger he poses.
The poet asks who could describe the host, stressing its enormous size and the limits of human speech.
Atropos herself is said to attack and overwhelm the seer's will, making fate an active enemy within him.
Eriphyle feigns modest mourning to hide greed, giving false reasons for putting away the necklace while she plots to keep it.
The gold begins great crimes and the Fury's laughter points ahead to Eriphyle's betrayal and her son's matricide.
Parents rejoicing at their sons' deaths exaggerates Spartan martial ideals to show fierce devotion to glory.
The narrator turns to address Amphiaraus and the river Alpheus directly, heightening the epic tone.
The horse marvelling at the lynx hides and its rider's weight paints Parthenopaeus as a boy playing at war.
Atalanta is compared to a tigress robbed of her cubs chasing the thief's horse, stressing her ferocious maternal desperation.
Her paired questions show she doubts his readiness and reveal her fear through disbelief.
The boar memory shows Parthenopaeus as brave but inexperienced, and Atalanta as a skilled, protective huntress.
Her promise that no mother's tears will call him back later hints at the tragedy of his death in war.
She turns from her son to address the Arcadians directly, accusing them of stony indifference and widening her private grief.
The king is compared to a wolf fleeing with blood on its mouth. The comparison conveys guilt and fear of pursuit.
Rumour is presented as an active agent that piles panic upon panic, showing how fear spreads.
The frenzied priestess addresses the absent Bacchus directly. This gives her prophecy urgency and a note of reproach.
The two bulls fighting over a pasture figure the brothers' war, and foreshadow their mutual destruction.
"Clear-sighted blindness" joins opposites to express Tiresias's inner vision.
Awe 'guards the silence' and the light is a 'phantom', making the grove seem haunted.
The frightened man is compared to a hunter awaiting a lion, conveying dread of the unseen approach.
Tiresias breaks off his threat, implying a terrible unspoken name and heightening the ritual's menace.
Rent shadows and belching mud give a vivid, grotesque picture of the underworld opening.
Vivid description of Cadmus' bloodless head and the drinking serpents makes the ghosts visible, and foreshadows Thebes' cursed origins.
Bristling hair and a pulsing pale face physically show the seer being filled with prophetic inspiration.
Tiresias is unsure whether his sudden vision comes from the dead or from Apollo, stressing his blind man's new sight.
Oedipus is called a living corpse joined with Death, expressing his blinded, wretched state as worse than dying.
Thebes will win, yet is possessed by Furies and Oedipus' curse, so victory is hollow; the prophecy is deliberately riddling.
Anger, Fury, Fear and Valour appear as Bacchus's followers, making his drunken army an allegory of his own nature.
The drying of the Argive land is compared to the Nile's ebb in Egypt, with the country waiting for the river's return.
The narrator openly anticipates Opheltes' death and the funeral games, casting a shadow over the tender scene that follows.
The nursing scene is likened to the infant Jupiter on Ide, with clashing cymbals and wails, adding mythic grandeur and unease.
The child's carefree play, unaware of danger, tells the reader he is doomed, which deepens the pathos.
The soldiers' cry for water is compared to sailors' shouts greeting Leucas, with the land echoing back, extending the scene beyond the battlefield.
Desperate thirst makes men trample their own princes and drown friends, so the rescuing water becomes a cause of harm.
The river is "plundered" and defiled like a victim, giving the stream a suffering body.
The drinking is likened to battle and sack of a city, turning a rescue into a scene of plunder and violence.
The prince addresses the river directly as a deity, praising its self-sustaining source in a formal hymn-like invocation.
